record.tranche_reason: Compares reconstruction error across SAE dictionary sizes, a different measurement relevant to the claim's assertion that error remains at larger scales. It does not measure linear predictability or overlap of residual errors across tokens.
record.gate_note: The reported SAE MSE values across dictionary sizes bear on error magnitude at finite scales. Feature-similarity statistics, feature swapping, and Frankenstein-SAE performance are not rows for the claim: they concern feature matching or the study's newly constructed models, not the specified properties of SAE residual errors.
record.test_reason: The post studies how SAE features change with dictionary width: novel versus split features, feature stitching, and 'Frankenstein' SAEs. It never examines the SAE error vector as an object. It does not regress error on input, compare per-token error norms across sizes, compare against random errors, separate linear from nonlinear error, or test circuits or steering with and without the error term. The only error numbers are aggregate MSEs in the set-up table describing the pre-trained SAEs used. These are descriptive statistics, not an experiment aimed at any version. Their being nonzero at every width does not test V2's claims about per-token predictability or shared failing contexts. The post predates and does not cite the original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that larger SAEs contain roughly 65% 'reconstruction' features, which are similar to or split from features in the smaller SAE and mainly reduce sparsity cost. The remaining ~35% are 'novel' features that add new information and reduce MSE. Adding the novel features to a smaller SAE improves its MSE (~10% for 768 vs 1536). Swapping in split features lowers L0. Stitched 'Frankenstein' SAEs beat same-size SAEs on MSE but at much higher L0. The authors note the 0.7 threshold is somewhat arbitrary and that generalization beyond these sites is unclear.
record.recipe_differences: Compares feature similarity and aggregate reconstruction MSE across SAE widths; does not use the original study's error-vector regression or per-token cross-size error analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported reconstruction MSE differs across dictionary sizes and model sites; the study does not report a sensitivity analysis of residual-error predictability.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggregate reconstruction MSE of GPT-2 layer-8 residual SAEs falls from 2.72 (768 features) to 1.144 (98,304 features). It stays well above zero across a 128x width range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregate SAE reconstruction error declines slowly with dictionary width and does not vanish in the tested range (descriptive only).

fits_no_version.finding: About 35% of larger-SAE features (max decoder cosine <= 0.7) are novel. Adding them to a smaller SAE lowers its MSE, by almost 10% for 657 features moved from GPT2-1536 into GPT2-768. The smaller SAE's MSE rises more on examples where such a novel feature fires (difference 0.589 vs 0.293).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Part of a small SAE's reconstruction error consists of features that larger SAEs learn. This loosely relates to V4's 'unlearned features', but the study does not separate linear from nonlinear error.

record.problems: The study does not measure residual-vector linear predictability or token-level error overlap across SAE sizes. It describes the 0.7 feature-similarity threshold as somewhat arbitrary and says generalization beyond the tested model sites and setups is unclear.
record.rows_left_out: Feature-cosine similarity distributions, feature-addition and swap effects, and Frankenstein-SAE results were left out because they concern feature matching or the study's new construction method rather than the claim's specified residual-error properties.

untested.parts: All: no regression of SAE error on input activations.
All: no per-token error-norm prediction across sizes and no test of shared failing contexts. Non-vanishing error appears only as descriptive aggregate MSE.
All: no comparison of SAE-splice loss against random errors of equal norm.
All: no split of error into linear and nonlinear parts.
All: no circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.
All: no comparison of training objectives or architectures on dark matter.

record.verdict_notes: The reader treated set-up table MSEs as a V2 test and gave a 'supports' label. That is removed: the table only describes the pre-trained SAEs used, and aggregate MSE cannot bear on per-token predictability or shared failure contexts. The relation enum has no exact 'neither tests nor uses' option. 'uses_without_test' is chosen because the study uses SAEs and reports their errors without testing any dark-matter version. The tranche is T6.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of the error vector is a linear function of the input activation.
The study reports aggregate MSE across dictionary sizes, but does not test per-token error-norm predictability across sizes or whether larger and smaller SAEs fail on the same contexts.
Whether SAE reconstruction errors harm model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether linear and nonlinear error components correspond to unlearned features and qualitatively different, hard-to-learn structure.
Whether SAE-feature-based analyses lose model behavior unless the error term is retained.
Whether dark matter is mainly a training artifact or shrinks with improved architectures or end-to-end training.
